query: Using the reported HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory high-entropy alloy as the starting material and its quasi-static properties—786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain—as the baseline, what single testable hypothesis proposes an intervention to overcome limited strain hardening, poor uniform deformability, and rapid failure as strain rate increases under adiabatic dynamic deformation? Specify the intervention and mechanism, predict changes relative to the baseline in strength, uniform deformation, localization resistance, and impact-induced energy release, define the strain-rate and loading conditions over which the prediction applies, cite supporting evidence from the reported refractory-alloy literature, and describe a matched baseline-versus-intervention experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a moderate amount of tungsten to the HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory HEA will promote the formation of a secondary, tungsten‐rich phase (or finely dispersed tungsten precipitates) that enhances dynamic strain hardening, increases uniform deformability, and delays adiabatic shear localization under high strain rate conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory HEA with a quasi‐static yield strength of 786 MPa, compressive strength of 1314 MPa, and fracture strain of 13.5%.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled tungsten addition into the alloy composition (e.g., targeting a modest atomic percent that can induce dual-phase microstructure) followed by a heat treatment designed to precipitate tungsten-rich secondary phases.
generation.conditions: Dynamic compression tests conducted under adiabatic conditions at room temperature with strain rates in the range of approximately 1300 s⁻¹ to 2100 s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine tungsten-rich precipitates or a dual-phase microstructure that acts as barriers to dislocation motion and impedes the early formation of adiabatic shear bands.
generation.mechanism: The high melting point and thermal stability of tungsten help mitigate thermal softening during high-speed deformation. The tungsten-rich phase increases dislocation storage capacity and enhances strain hardening, thereby delaying the onset of localization and improving uniform ductility under dynamic loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the tungsten-modified alloy is expected to exhibit a moderate increase in dynamic yield strength (potentially a 10–20% improvement), enhanced uniform plastic deformation (an increase in fracture strain under dynamic conditions), improved resistance to adiabatic shear localization, and a more controlled impact-induced energy release.
generation.baseline: The original HfZrTiTa0.53 refractory HEA with quasi‐static properties: 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% fracture strain.
generation.boundary: The predicted improvements are expected under dynamic, adiabatic conditions at strain rates between 1300 s⁻¹ and 2100 s⁻¹ at room temperature. The effect may differ outside this strain-rate range or under different thermal environments.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum tungsten content and heat-treatment protocol required to reliably induce the beneficial dual-phase microstructure are not precisely defined. Quantitative gains in yield strength and ductility under dynamic loading remain uncertain until detailed microstructural characterization and mechanical testing are performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy and one set with the added tungsten and appropriate heat treatment to form the secondary tungsten-rich phase. Subject both sample sets to dynamic compression tests using a Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar at strain rates in the range 1300 s⁻¹ to 2100 s⁻¹ under adiabatic conditions at room temperature.
measurements: Work hardening rate / strain hardening behavior
Onset and development of adiabatic shear bands (via high-speed imaging or post-mortem microstructural analysis)
Impact-induced energy release characteristics (e.g., energy absorption metrics)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant improvement in dynamic yield strength, uniform deformability (i.e., increased fracture strain or extended work hardening regime), and delayed shear localization (or comparable impact energy absorption) relative to the baseline alloy under the specified dynamic conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

This study demonstrates that the addition of W significantly enhances the mechanical properties of TiZrMo alloys, with the phase ratio effectively being controlled by adjusting the elemental composition. As a result, a dual-phase Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA was successfully fabricated and subjected to comprehensive quasi-static and dynamic loading experiments to evaluate its energy release capability and mechanical properties for potential structural applications. The Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA demonstrated exceptional quasi-static mechanical performance, with a yield strength of 1490 MPa, an ultimate strength of 2200 MPa, and a fracture strain of 30%. Under dynamic loading at a strain rate of 3000 s−1, the alloy exhibited an even higher ultimate strength of 2300 MPa and maintained a fracture strain of 24%, showcasing its remarkable ability to retain plasticity under extreme conditions. Additionally, the Ti40Zr40Mo10W10 HEA displayed significant chemical energy release and a high energy release capacity.
